title: PostgreSQL connection refused after deployment
incident_log:
ERROR 2026-09-24 03:42:11 [order-service] Failed to connect to PostgreSQL after 3 retries
psycopg2.OperationalError: could not connect to server: Connection refused
    Is the server running on host "db-prod-01" (10.0.1.45) and accepting TCP/IP connections on port 5432?
CRITICAL: Order processing halted. 847 requests queued.
Last successful DB connection: 2026-09-24 03:38:44
Recent deployment: order-service v2.4.1 deployed at 03:35:00
actual_root_cause: The PostgreSQL server on host db-prod-01 (10.0.1.45:5432) is refusing TCP connections, causing order-service to halt all order processing after exhausting 3 connection retries.
actual_summary: Order processing is fully halted because the order-service cannot establish a TCP connection to the PostgreSQL database on db-prod-01, resulting in 847 queued and unprocessed requests. The database became unreachable approximately 3–4 minutes after the deployment of order-service v2.4.1, making a deployment-introduced misconfiguration (e.g., wrong host, port, or credentials) or a DB-side crash triggered by the new release the most likely root causes. Immediate actions should include verifying the PostgreSQL process status on db-prod-01 and reviewing any connection configuration changes in v2.4.1, with rollback to v2.4.0 as a candidate remediation if the deployment is implicated.
fix_summary: Order processing is fully halted due to the PostgreSQL server on db-prod-01 (10.0.1.45:5432) refusing TCP connections, blocking 847 queued orders. The immediate priority is to determine whether the DB process crashed (and safely restart it) or whether the v2.4.1 deployment introduced a connection misconfiguration — both must be investigated in parallel given the 7-minute timing correlation. If DB restoration alone does not resolve the issue, rollback of order-service to v2.4.0 is the recommended remediation path while the root cause is fully investigated.

actual_summary: The payment-service pod was killed by Kubernetes with exit code 137 (OOMKill) after consuming nearly all of its 512Mi memory limit. This occurred approximately 15 minutes after the v3.1.0 deployment, strongly suggesting the new release introduced a memory regression — either a leak, an oversized cache, or increased baseline memory usage. Immediate remediation options include rolling back to the previous version and/or increasing the pod memory limit while the root cause in the new code is investigated.
fix_summary: The payment-service experienced an OOMKill almost certainly caused by a memory regression introduced in the v3.1.0 deployment 15 minutes prior, exhausting the pod's 512Mi memory limit. The primary fix is to immediately roll back to the previous stable version via `kubectl rollout undo deployment/payment-service`, optionally combined with a temporary memory limit increase to 1Gi as a safety buffer. Concurrently, the v3.1.0 code diff must be reviewed for memory leaks, oversized caches, or unbounded data loading to prevent recurrence when v3.1.0 is re-deployed after a fix.

title: Redis cache connection failure
incident_log:
ERROR 2026-09-24 11:05:22 [session-service] Redis connection failed
redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to redis-prod:6379. Connection refused.
Cache miss rate: 100% (normal: 2%)
Response times increased from 45ms to 890ms
Redis process status: unknown
Last successful cache operation: 2026-09-24 11:02:15
actual_root_cause: The Redis server at redis-prod:6379 is refusing connections, most likely due to a crashed or stopped Redis process, causing a 100% cache miss rate and significant response time degradation in the session-service.
actual_summary: The Redis cache server at redis-prod:6379 stopped accepting connections at approximately 11:02:15, with the session-service fully unable to reach it by 11:05:22. This caused the cache miss rate to spike to 100% (from a normal 2%), driving response times up nearly 20x from 45ms to 890ms. The root cause is a Redis process failure of unknown origin; without a functioning cache, every request is falling through to the underlying data layer.
fix_summary: The Redis process on redis-prod:6379 has crashed or stopped, causing the session-service to fall through to the backing data store for every request, resulting in a 20x response time increase. The immediate priority is to SSH into redis-prod, diagnose the crash cause via logs, and restart the Redis service — then verify the cache miss rate and response times return to baseline. This is rated medium risk because a blind restart carries some data integrity considerations, and the backing store remains under stress until the cache is repopulated.

title: Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff after deployment

WARN 2026-09-24 16:30:44 [auth-service] Pod auth-service-6bc9d-p8k2x CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl describe pod auth-service-6bc9d-p8k2x:
  Reason: CrashLoopBackOff
  Restart Count: 5
Last log before crash:
  ERROR: DATABASE_URL environment variable is not set
  Failed to initialize connection pool
  Application startup failed — exit code 1
Recent deployment: auth-service v2.0.0 at 16:25:00
actual_root_cause: The auth-service v2.0.0 deployment is missing the DATABASE_URL environment variable in its pod spec, causing the application to fail initialization and enter CrashLoopBackOff.
actual_summary: The auth-service entered CrashLoopBackOff (5 restarts) immediately after the v2.0.0 deployment at 16:25:00 because the DATABASE_URL environment variable is absent from the new pod spec, preventing the connection pool from initializing. The application exits with code 1 on every startup attempt, making authentication fully unavailable. This is a bad deployment — the fix is to either roll back to the previous version or patch the deployment to restore the missing DATABASE_URL environment variable.
fix_summary: The auth-service v2.0.0 deployment is missing the DATABASE_URL environment variable, causing every pod startup to fail with exit code 1 and rendering authentication completely unavailable. The immediate fix is to roll back to the previous deployment version via `kubectl rollout undo deployment/auth-service`, which should restore service within minutes; if rollback is blocked by a schema migration, the alternative is to patch DATABASE_URL into the v2.0.0 deployment from the correct Kubernetes Secret. After service is restored, the v2.0.0 manifest must be corrected in source control and pre-flight config validation added to the deployment pipeline to prevent recurrence.

title: Slow database queries causing API timeout
incident_log:
WARN 2026-09-24 13:15:08 [api-service] Request timeout on /api/orders
Database query exceeded 5000ms threshold
Affected endpoint: GET /api/orders?user_id=*
Query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC
Execution time: 8200ms (normal: 45ms)
DB CPU: 94% (normal: 20%)
Table orders: 45M rows
No recent deployment
Autovacuum last run: 12 days ago
actual_root_cause: The orders table (45M rows) is suffering from severe bloat and stale statistics due to autovacuum not running for 12 days, causing the query planner to choose a full or inefficient scan on GET /api/orders, driving DB CPU to 94% and query execution time from 45ms to 8200ms.
actual_summary: The GET /api/orders endpoint began timing out after query execution time spiked from a normal 45ms to 8200ms, pushing DB CPU to 94%. The most likely cause is that autovacuum has not run in 12 days on the 45M-row orders table, resulting in excessive dead tuple bloat, stale planner statistics, and potentially a degraded or abandoned index — causing the database to fall back to an expensive scan. Manually triggering VACUUM ANALYZE on the orders table and verifying composite index coverage on (user_id, created_at) are the immediate recommended actions.

runbooks_retrieved.title: High Database Query Latency / Slow Queries
Data Pipeline Failure / ETL Job Error

fix_summary: The immediate priority is to run VACUUM ANALYZE on the orders table to purge 12 days of dead tuple bloat and refresh planner statistics, which should cause the query planner to revert from an expensive scan back to the expected index scan and restore GET /api/orders latency to normal. In parallel, confirm the composite index on (user_id, created_at) is present and valid, kill any long-running blocking queries, and apply a statement_timeout guard to prevent continued DB CPU saturation during recovery. After service is restored, fix the root autovacuum scheduling issue to prevent recurrence.

actual_root_cause: The JWT secret was rotated in auth-service at 09:55:00 but api-gateway and payment-service were not updated with the new secret, causing 100% signature verification failures on all authenticated endpoints.
actual_summary: A JWT secret rotation applied exclusively to auth-service at 09:55:00 left api-gateway and payment-service using the old secret, causing a complete 100% authentication failure across all protected endpoints. Every token issued by the updated auth-service is now signed with the new secret but rejected by the out-of-date verifiers, fully blocking authenticated user access. The fastest path to resolution is rolling auth-service back to the old secret (restoring immediate compatibility) or simultaneously pushing the new secret to api-gateway and payment-service if rollback is not feasible. Secret consistency across all three services must be confirmed before declaring the incident resolved.

title: Cascading timeout across microservices
incident_log:
ERROR 2026-09-24 15:22:44 [order-service] Upstream timeout
HTTPError: 504 Gateway Timeout from inventory-service
order-service thread pool: 98% utilized
Response times: order-service 8200ms, inventory-service 6100ms, pricing-service 5800ms
All services degraded simultaneously
Root alert: pricing-service CPU 99% starting at 15:18:00
No circuit breaker configured on any service
actual_root_cause: pricing-service CPU saturation at 99% (starting 15:18:00) caused response time degradation that propagated upstream through inventory-service and order-service via synchronous calls, exhausting the order-service thread pool (98%) and resulting in 504 Gateway Timeouts for end users.
actual_summary: A CPU saturation event on pricing-service (99% CPU from 15:18:00) caused its response times to balloon to ~5800ms, which cascaded synchronously through inventory-service (6100ms) and ultimately into order-service (8200ms), triggering 504 Gateway Timeout errors for customers. The absence of circuit breakers, bulkheads, or fallback logic on any service meant there was no mechanism to isolate the failure, allowing a single service's resource exhaustion to degrade the entire order flow. Immediate remediation should include shedding load on pricing-service, enabling circuit breakers, and investigating the root cause of the CPU spike.
fix_summary: The immediate priority is to break the synchronous failure cascade by isolating pricing-service (via circuit breaker or fallback response) and restarting it to clear CPU saturation, then restarting order-service to drain the near-exhausted thread pool and restore end-user request handling. These actions address the active blast radius while the root cause of the pricing-service CPU spike (starting 15:18:00) is investigated in parallel. Long-term, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and fallback logic must be implemented across all three services — their absence was the primary architectural factor that turned a single-service CPU event into a customer-facing 504 outage.
postmortem_title: Cascading 504 Gateway Timeout Outage — Order Service — 2026-09-24

title: Intermittent 502s with no obvious cause

Error rate: 3.2% (threshold: 1%)

actual_root_cause: The load balancer or an upstream gateway component is periodically failing to route requests, likely due to connection pool exhaustion, a misconfigured health check interval, or a flapping backend instance that passes health checks but fails real traffic — manifesting as 30-second burst 502 errors every 8-10 minutes.
actual_summary: Intermittent 502 errors are occurring in 30-second bursts every 8-10 minutes across all /api/* endpoints, with a 3.2% error rate. The regular periodicity, passing health checks, and random endpoint distribution point to a gateway or load balancer layer issue — most likely connection pool recycling, a flapping backend node, or a periodic resource saturation event rather than an application code problem. The slightly elevated latency supports a degraded network or infrastructure path as a contributing condition.
fix_summary: The incident involves intermittent 502 errors in regular 30-second bursts every 8-10 minutes across all /api/* endpoints, most likely caused by connection pool recycling, a flapping backend node that passes superficial health checks, or a periodic scheduled process saturating gateway resources. Immediate focus should be on identifying the flapping or resource-saturating component via gateway logs and load balancer metrics, draining any unhealthy backend, and tightening health checks so failing nodes are removed before they impact real traffic. No application code changes are indicated — this is an infrastructure/configuration layer problem requiring targeted gateway and load balancer remediation.

title: CDN serving stale assets after deployment
incident_log:
WARN 2026-09-24 11:45:33 [frontend-monitoring] Users reporting stale UI
Symptom: Users seeing old version of checkout page after v4.2.0 deployment
Deployment completed: 11:30:00
Cache invalidation triggered: yes, at 11:31:00
CloudFront invalidation status: completed
But users in EU still seeing old assets
Asset URLs: versioned (e.g. main.a3f9b2.js)
CDN edge nodes: 47 globally
EU edge propagation: potentially incomplete
actual_root_cause: CloudFront cache invalidation has not fully propagated to EU edge nodes after the v4.2.0 deployment, causing EU users to receive stale versioned assets from incompletely updated edge caches.
actual_summary: After the v4.2.0 frontend deployment, EU users continue to see the old checkout page because CloudFront cache invalidation has not fully propagated to EU edge nodes, even though the invalidation was reported as globally complete. The impact is geographically scoped to EU users and does not affect core backend functionality, making this a medium-severity degradation. The root issue is likely a propagation lag or a partially stale HTML document serving old versioned asset URLs, rather than a failure of the invalidation itself.
fix_summary: EU users are receiving the stale v4.2.0 checkout page because CloudFront cache invalidation has not fully propagated to EU edge nodes, likely due to propagation lag that was incorrectly reported as complete. The immediate fix is to trigger a fresh, explicitly scoped CloudFront invalidation targeting HTML and the affected versioned JS asset (main.a3f9b2.js), then verify EU edge nodes are serving fresh content via geo-targeted curl tests and CloudFront metrics. If propagation continues to lag beyond 15 minutes, temporarily bypass EU edge caching by routing directly to the S3 origin to restore service while the CDN catches up.
postmortem_title: CloudFront EU Edge Propagation Failure — Frontend Checkout Page — 2026-09-24
